Good for breaking a blank page at the start of a brand exploration; not a system. Take the direction, then build the real scale in OKLCH.
Trained on one person's picks, so it becomes that person's palette generator, not the studio's.

entries.name: Relume
entries.what: Generates a sitemap from a company description, then wireframes each page from a library of several thousand Figma and Webflow components, so a whole site structure exists before design starts.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with limited generations; paid plans on the site's pricing page, figures not published in the served HTML.
notes: The sitemap-first workflow matches how a marketing site project actually starts, and it produces something a client can argue with on day one instead of week two.
The component library is Webflow-shaped. It fits that pipeline far better than it fits ours.
Everything it makes looks like Relume. Fine as structure, a problem if the visual language survives to the deliverable.

entries.name: Midjourney
entries.what: Image generation model with the strongest aesthetic defaults of the mainstream options — style references, character consistency and a web editor, still with a large Discord community around it.
entries.priceDetail: No free tier. Subscription plans, with figures not published in the served pricing page — check in-app before committing.
notes: Still the best default look of the mainstream generators, which matters for mood boards and concept imagery where nothing beats fewer prompts to something usable.
No free tier, and no commercial usage below the paid plans. Check the current terms before anything generated reaches a client deliverable.
Provenance is the standing risk on any generated image in client work. Use it for internal exploration, and be deliberate about what ships.

entries.name: Recraft
entries.what: Image model built for designers rather than illustrators — generates true vector output and editable SVG, holds a consistent brand style across a set, and does text-in-image reliably.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with limited credits; paid plans priced per credit allowance, figures not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Vector output is the reason to pick it over Midjourney for our work — an SVG icon set or illustration can be edited, recoloured and shipped, where a PNG cannot.
The brand-style feature keeps a set coherent, which is the usual failure of generated assets across a whole site.
Same provenance caution as any generated asset. Treat vector output as a base to redraw from, not a final mark.

entries.name: Krea
entries.what: Real-time generative canvas — sketch or arrange shapes and the image regenerates as you move things, plus upscaling, video and 3D asset tools with several models behind one interface.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $9, $35 and $105/month.
notes: Real-time control is the interesting part: steering an image by moving shapes is closer to designing than to writing prompts and hoping.
Several models behind one subscription is cheaper than holding accounts with each, if generated imagery becomes routine here.
Enhance and upscale are the features we would use most in practice, on assets a client supplied at the wrong resolution.

entries.name: Remove.bg
entries.what: Background removal in about five seconds, with an API and Photoshop, Figma and CLI integrations — the reference implementation of the one job it does.
entries.priceDetail: Free for low-resolution previews in the browser; full-resolution downloads and API access are credit-based.
notes: Still the most reliable at hair and soft edges, which is where the free alternatives fail and where a client notices.
The API is the part worth remembering: cutting out a few hundred product images in a build is a script, not an afternoon.
Free tier gives low resolution only. Budget credits if a project needs full-size output.

entries.name: Upscayl
entries.what: Free, open-source image upscaler for macOS, Windows and Linux that runs entirely on your own machine — no upload, no account, several models to choose from.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source; a paid Pro build exists at around $25 for extra features.
notes: Runs locally, which makes it the right answer for a client's unreleased product photography — nothing is uploaded to anyone's server.
Solves a constant real problem: the logo or photo a client sends at 400px that needs to be a hero image.
Needs a reasonably capable GPU to be quick, and upscaling invents detail. Check the result at full size before it ships.

entries.name: Lummi
entries.what: Stock library of AI-generated photos, illustrations and 3D assets, royalty-free, curated for a consistent modern look rather than the usual stock-photo register.
entries.priceDetail: Free downloads with an account; a paid tier removes limits. Figures not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Fills the gap between generating imagery ourselves and paying for traditional stock, with a look that suits product marketing pages.
Curated, so the hit rate is far better than prompting from scratch when you need one specific image now.
Generated imagery with the usual provenance caveat, and a real risk that a competitor's site uses the same picture. Check before it becomes a hero.

entries.name: Retool
entries.what: Internal-tool builder: drag together tables, forms and charts, wire them to any database or API with JavaScript in between, and ship an admin panel in hours rather than sprints.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $5 and $10 per user/month, with $50/user tiers for business features.
notes: Directly relevant to how we scope: clients ask for an admin panel on top of every build, and building one properly costs weeks that add nothing to their product.
Self-hosting is available, which is what makes it viable when the data cannot leave the client's infrastructure.
It becomes a dependency the client pays for forever. Say so during scoping — the alternative is us maintaining a bespoke admin panel forever instead.

entries.name: FlutterFlow
entries.what: Visual builder for Flutter apps — design screens, wire up Firebase or a custom backend, and export real Dart source or publish to the App Store and Play Store directly.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $39/month, with $55 and $80/month team tiers.
notes: Source export is what separates it from most app builders: a client is not stranded if they leave, and we can take the Dart into a normal build.
One codebase for iOS and Android suits the scale of app work we get asked for, where a native team for each is not in the budget.
Flutter, not React Native — so it does not share components or people with our web work. That is the real cost of choosing it.

entries.name: Descript
entries.what: Edits video and audio by editing the transcript — delete a sentence and the footage goes with it. Also removes filler words, generates captions and clones a voice for corrections.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid at $16, $24, $35 and $50/month per user depending on features and export quality.
notes: Text-based editing is genuinely faster for the talking-head and walkthrough content we make — case study videos, client updates, internal explainers.
Filler-word removal and captions in one pass covers most of what a demo video needs before it is presentable.
Voice cloning needs a clear internal rule on consent before anyone uses it on a client's recorded voice.

entries.name: CapCut
entries.what: Free video editor with auto-captions, background removal and a large template library, on desktop, web and mobile. Made by ByteDance, the company behind TikTok.
entries.priceDetail: Free with a watermark on some exports and templates; a Pro subscription removes limits.
notes: Rated Low for studio work but listed because it is what social content is actually cut in, and a client's marketing team will already be using it.
ByteDance ownership and its terms around uploaded content make it the wrong place for anything confidential or pre-launch.
Auto-captions are good enough to be worth it for social cuts; everything else we would do in Descript or Screen Studio.

entries.name: GitHub Copilot
entries.what: Completion, chat and a coding agent wired into GitHub itself — assign an issue and it opens a pull request, review in the same place the code already lives.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with monthly completion and chat limits. Paid from $4/month (Pro), with usage rates around $0.04–$0.18 per premium request above the allowance.
notes: The reason to care is not the completions, it is that the agent lives where the repo, the issues and the reviews already are — no extra tool for a client's own developers to adopt.
Cheapest paid tier of any of these at $4/month, and free tier now exists, so there is no cost argument for a client's team not having it.
Weaker than Claude Code or Cursor on multi-file work. Fine as the baseline everyone has, not the tool for a hard refactor.

entries.name: Zed
entries.what: Editor written in Rust by the people who made Atom and Tree-sitter — GPU-rendered, genuinely fast on large files, with multiplayer editing and agent panels built in rather than bolted on.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. Paid plans at $10 and $30/month cover hosted agent usage; bring your own API key and it stays free.
notes: The speed is real and noticeable on a big Next.js repo, which is where VS Code and its forks start to drag.
Open source with bring-your-own-key, so the editor is not tied to a model vendor — worth knowing when a client dictates which provider we may use.
Smaller extension ecosystem than VS Code. Check the language support a project needs before switching anyone over.

entries.name: Warp
entries.what: Terminal rebuilt as a modern app — blocks instead of a scrollback soup, editable input, and an agent that can run and chain commands, now positioned as a platform for running coding agents.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $20/month, with a $200/month tier for heavier agent usage.
notes: Command blocks are the quality-of-life win: sharing the exact command and its output with someone is a copy, not a screenshot of a wall of text.
The agent-platform pivot is recent and the pricing follows usage. Try the free tier before anyone commits.
It sees every command you run, including ones with client credentials in them. Check what leaves the machine before pointing it at production.

entries.name: Windsurf
entries.what: Agentic editor now built around managing several local and cloud agents from one surface — plan, delegate, review and merge without leaving the editor.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $20/month, with $80/month per-seat team pricing and a $200/month tier.
notes: Same idea as Conductor, solved inside the editor rather than around it: several agents at once without them treading on each other.
Formerly Codeium, and the product has changed shape more than once. Older write-ups describe a different tool.
One of three or four editors making the same claim right now. Pick one to trial properly rather than sampling all of them.

entries.name: Codex
entries.what: OpenAI's coding agent inside ChatGPT — hand it a task or a pull request and it works in its own sandbox, returning a diff to review. Also a CLI.
entries.priceDetail: Included with paid ChatGPT plans rather than sold separately; no standalone price is published.
notes: Worth having as the second opinion: on a stubborn bug, a different model in a different harness often sees what the first one missed.
Bundled into a ChatGPT subscription, so for anyone here already paying there is nothing extra to buy.
Sandboxed cloud execution means client code on OpenAI's infrastructure. Check the contract before pointing it at a client repo.

entries.name: Ollama
entries.what: Runs open-weight models locally with one command — `ollama run llama3` pulls and serves a model on your own machine, with an OpenAI-compatible API on localhost.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source to run locally. Paid cloud plans at $20/month and $100/month, plus a $200/year option.
notes: The answer to any client whose data cannot leave their network: the model runs on the machine, nothing is sent anywhere, and the API is OpenAI-shaped so our own code barely changes.
Also the cheapest way to develop against an LLM — no per-token bill while iterating on a prompt or a pipeline.
Local models are meaningfully weaker than frontier hosted ones. It buys compliance and iteration cost, not capability.

entries.name: LM Studio
entries.what: Desktop app for running local models with a proper interface — browse and download from Hugging Face, chat, and expose a local server, without touching a terminal.
entries.priceDetail: Free to download and run locally, with usage-priced cloud features from around $0.03 per unit.
notes: The GUI is why it is here alongside Ollama: it is the version a designer or a client can be shown, where Ollama is a command line.
Model browsing with quantisation and memory estimates saves the usual trial and error of finding a model that fits the machine.
The product is drifting toward its own agent offering. The local-model runner is the part to rely on.

entries.name: Replicate
entries.what: Runs thousands of open-source models behind one cloud API, billed by the second — image, video, audio and language models without provisioning a GPU or writing serving code.
entries.priceDetail: Pay per second of compute, with published unit rates from around $0.0002 to $0.04 per run depending on the model and hardware. Free credits to start.
notes: The right answer when a client build needs one specific model — background removal, upscaling, transcription — and we do not want to own inference infrastructure for it.
Per-second billing means a prototype costs pennies, and a viral client feature costs real money. Put a cap and a queue in front of it before launch.
Cold starts on less-used models can be tens of seconds. Test latency with the actual model before promising a live user experience.

entries.name: Modal
entries.what: Serverless compute for Python — decorate a function, and it runs in the cloud on CPU or GPU with the container built for you. Sub-second cold starts, billed per second.
entries.priceDetail: Usage-based, with published rates from around $0.001 per second of compute. Free monthly credits to start.
notes: Solves the awkward middle of client work: a batch job or a model that will not fit in a Vercel function but does not justify running a server.
The developer experience is genuinely good — no Dockerfile, no Kubernetes, and the same code runs locally.
Python only, which puts it outside our usual TypeScript stack. That is the cost of the convenience.

entries.name: Groq
entries.what: Inference provider running open models on its own custom silicon, with output speeds far above GPU-based hosts — an OpenAI-compatible API for the models it carries.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with rate limits, then per-token pricing. Enterprise deals published only as contact-us.
notes: Speed changes what a feature can be: at Groq's rates a model call is fast enough to sit inside a keystroke-level interaction rather than behind a spinner.
Limited to the open models they host, so it is a complement to Claude rather than a replacement.
Their free tier is generous enough to prototype on, which is the cheapest way to find out whether latency was the real blocker.

entries.name: Dify
entries.what: Open-source platform for building agentic workflows — visual pipeline builder, retrieval over your own documents, model routing and an API per app, self-hostable.
entries.priceDetail: Apache-2.0 and free to self-host. Hosted plans published at $590 and $1,590, with smaller tiers on the site.
notes: Directly relevant to the work clients keep asking for: a chat or retrieval feature over their own documents, without us writing the whole orchestration layer.
Apache-2.0 and self-hostable means a client's documents can stay on their infrastructure — the usual blocker on this kind of build.
A visual builder becomes the source of truth, which is harder to review and version than code. Decide that deliberately before it holds anything important.

entries.name: Flowise
entries.what: Open-source drag-and-drop builder for LLM apps and agents — chain models, tools, retrieval and memory on a canvas, then expose the result as an API or embeddable chat.
entries.priceDetail: Open source and free to self-host; a hosted cloud tier is sold on top.
notes: Its use for us is speed of demonstration: a working retrieval prototype in an afternoon that a client can try, before anyone commits to a build.
Overlaps heavily with Dify. Dify is the more finished product; Flowise is lighter to stand up.
Prototype tooling, not a production dependency. What ships should be code we own.

entries.name: CrewAI
entries.what: Python framework for multi-agent systems — define agents with roles, give them tools and tasks, and orchestrate them in sequence or in parallel, with a hosted control plane on top.
entries.priceDetail: Open-source framework, free. Hosted platform pricing is not published on the site.
notes: Worth knowing as the vocabulary rather than the tool: role, task, crew is how most multi-agent work is now described, and clients arrive using those words.
Multi-agent orchestration is usually premature — one well-prompted agent with good tools beats a crew of five for most real jobs, at a fraction of the token cost.
Python, and the hosted tier's pricing is unpublished. Treat the framework as the useful part.

entries.name: Vapi
entries.what: Developer platform for voice agents — handles telephony, streaming speech recognition, interruption handling and text-to-speech, so a phone-answering agent is an API integration rather than a stack.
entries.priceDetail: Usage-based from around $0.05 per minute, with published figures at $1, $2 and $10 tiers of prepaid credit. Free credit to start.
notes: Real client demand sits here — a business wanting its phone answered out of hours — and the hard parts (latency, interruptions, telephony) are exactly what this sells.
Per-minute billing on a phone line is a runaway cost if a loop misbehaves. Cap spend and set a maximum call length before anything goes live.
Voice agents need a clear disclosure to the caller. That is a legal question for the client, and it belongs in the scope, not in the build.

entries.name: Canva
entries.what: Browser design tool built around templates and brand kits, with AI generation, video and print output — the thing a client's marketing team already uses.
entries.priceDetail: Genuinely usable free tier. Paid Pro and Teams plans per seat; current figures were not in the served pricing page.
notes: Listed because of who uses it, not because we design in it: handing a client a Canva brand kit is often the difference between the identity surviving and it being rebuilt badly in PowerPoint.
Brand kits with locked colours and fonts are the practical handover artefact — cheaper to maintain than policing a style guide nobody opens.
Output quality falls off fast outside templates. It is a containment strategy for client-made assets, not a design tool for our own work.

entries.name: Vizcom
entries.what: Turns a rough sketch into a photorealistic render in seconds, keeping the drawn lines as the structure — built for industrial and product designers rather than for prompt-only image generation.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $49/month.
notes: Sketch-driven rather than prompt-driven, which is the interesting bit: the designer controls the form and the model only handles the rendering.
Rated Low because we build software, not physical products. It earns its place if a client project ever touches hardware or packaging.
$49/month is steep for occasional use; the free tier is the right way to find out whether it fits a project.

entries.name: Airtable
entries.what: Database that behaves like a spreadsheet — typed fields, linked records, views, automations and an API, with an app-building layer on top.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with record limits. Team $20/user/month, Business $45/user/month, both billed annually.
notes: Where most client projects actually start: their operational data already lives in an Airtable, and its API is often the fastest legitimate backend for phase one.
Per-user pricing at $20–$45 makes it expensive as a client's permanent system, and record limits bite sooner than they expect. Plan the migration path at the start.
Treat it as a source to read from, not the architecture. Building a client's product on Airtable is a decision to explain, not a default.

entries.name: Bubble
entries.what: Full no-code app platform — visual editor for interface, database and logic, with hosting and a plugin ecosystem, now with AI generation for a first draft.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier to build. Paid plans by workload units rather than seats; current figures were not in the served pricing page.
notes: Worth knowing because prospects arrive with a Bubble app they have outgrown — reading one to understand the intended product is a real skill on rebuild work.
Rated Low as a build tool for us: we cannot version it, review it or hand it over as code, which is most of what a client pays us for.
Workload-unit pricing is genuinely hard to forecast, and it is the usual reason a Bubble app becomes a rebuild.

entries.name: Glide
entries.what: Builds internal business apps from a spreadsheet or database — connect Airtable, Sheets or SQL and it generates a usable mobile and web app with roles and permissions.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $25/month and $125/month.
notes: The honest use is scoping: build the client's internal tool in Glide in a day, watch which parts they actually use, then quote the real build against evidence.
Cheaper than Retool at the low end and far less capable. Glide for a form-and-list app, Retool when there is real logic.
If it survives as the permanent answer, that is a good outcome for the client — say so rather than quietly upselling a build.

entries.name: Plasmic
entries.what: Visual builder that works against your own React codebase — designers assemble pages from your real components, and the output is code in your repo rather than an export.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month. Paid at $39/month and $103/month, with a $399/month tier for larger teams.
notes: The closest of these to how we work: it composes our components rather than generating fresh markup, so the design system stays the source of truth.
The realistic use is letting a client's marketing team build landing pages from components we shipped, without a deploy for every headline change.
It becomes part of the build pipeline, so removing it later means rebuilding those pages. Scope that honestly at the start.

entries.name: Runway
entries.what: Generative video platform — text and image to video, plus editing tools like background removal, motion brush and camera control, aimed at people producing finished work rather than clips.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier with limited credits. Paid from $12/month, with higher credit tiers above.
notes: The one generative video tool here with a real editing surface rather than a prompt box, which is what makes it usable for a client hero video or a title sequence.
Credits run down quickly at higher resolutions. Budget per project rather than assuming the subscription covers it.
Same provenance question as generated imagery, and more visible on video. Be deliberate about what reaches a client's brand.

entries.name: Miro
entries.what: Infinite collaborative whiteboard with the workshop furniture — sticky notes, voting, timers, templates for retros and journey maps, and presentation mode.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier with three editable boards. Paid from $8/user/month.
notes: The practical case is client workshops: discovery sessions, journey mapping and prioritisation run better on a board everyone can edit than in a document.
The free tier's three-board limit is the catch on a studio with several clients running at once.
For a quick diagram on a call, tldraw or Excalidraw are faster and need no account. Miro earns its place for facilitated sessions.

entries.name: Whimsical
entries.what: Fast tool for the four diagram types product work actually needs — flowcharts, wireframes, mind maps and sticky notes — with deliberately constrained styling so diagrams stay consistent.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier with a board limit. Paid from $10/month per editor.
notes: Constrained styling is the feature: nobody can spend an hour making a flowchart pretty, so the diagram gets made and the meeting moves on.
Its wireframe mode is the fastest route from a conversation to something structural a client can react to, before Figma is involved.
Diagrams live in Whimsical's cloud. Export the ones that matter into the handover repo.

entries.name: Arc
entries.what: Browser built around spaces and profiles rather than a single strip of tabs — separate windows of context per project, with split view and a command bar.
entries.priceDetail: Free.
notes: Spaces map onto client work well: one space per client with its own tabs, logins and profile, instead of forty tabs and the wrong account signed in.
Profile separation is the practical bit — being signed into a client's Google account and ours at once without constant switching.
The Browser Company has moved its attention to a newer product, so treat Arc as stable rather than actively developed.

entries.name: Loom
entries.what: Async video messaging — record screen and camera, get a link immediately, with transcripts, comments and viewer analytics. Now owned by Atlassian.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier with limits on video length and library size. Business from $18/user/month.
notes: Still the default for client updates, and clients recognise the format — a three-minute walkthrough answers questions a written status report generates.
Viewer analytics tell you whether a client actually watched, which is quietly useful before a review call.
Recordings sit on Atlassian's servers. Cap, already on this list, is the self-hostable alternative when a walkthrough shows something confidential.

entries.name: Fathom
entries.what: Meeting recorder and note-taker for Zoom, Meet and Teams — joins the call, transcribes, and produces summaries and action items, with CRM sync on paid tiers.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with unlimited recording and transcription. Paid from $15/user/month, with $19 and $34/month tiers.
notes: Unusually generous free tier — unlimited recording where most competitors cap it — which makes it the cheapest way to stop taking notes in client calls.
It joins as a visible bot, unlike Granola. That is more honest in a client meeting and more intrusive in a sales one; pick per call.
Recording a client call needs their consent regardless of the tool. Get it at the top of the call, not in the terms.

entries.name: NotebookLM
entries.what: Google's research notebook grounded in sources you upload — it answers only from those documents with citations back to the passage, and generates summaries, briefing docs and audio overviews.
entries.priceDetail: Free with a Google account; higher limits come with paid Google AI plans.
notes: Grounding is the whole point: answers cite the passage they came from, so a client's brand guidelines or a 90-page tender can be interrogated without the model inventing clauses.
Directly useful on the work we do — reading a client's existing documentation, specs and research before a kickoff, and getting a briefing doc out of it.
Uploading a client's documents to Google is a processing decision. Check the contract, and use the paid Workspace tier where data terms matter.

entries.name: Elicit
entries.what: Research assistant over 125 million academic papers — searches semantically, extracts findings and methods into a table across many papers at once, and summarises with citations.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid from $11/month, with $39/month and annual plans at $132 and $468.
notes: Narrow for us, but real when a client project needs an evidence base — accessibility research, behavioural claims in marketing copy, anything a regulator might ask about.
The extract-to-table feature is the time saver: twenty papers' methods and findings side by side instead of twenty PDFs.
Rated Low because most weeks we have no use for it. Worth knowing it exists rather than subscribing.

entries.name: Adobe Firefly
entries.what: Adobe's generative image, video and audio models, trained on Adobe Stock and licensed content, with indemnification offered for enterprise use and Content Credentials attached to output.
entries.priceDetail: Limited free generations; included with Creative Cloud subscriptions, with credit-based tiers above.
notes: The training data is the reason this outranks better-looking models for client work: Adobe offers indemnification on enterprise plans, which is the only real answer to a client asking who owns the image.
Content Credentials embed provenance in the file, which is becoming a procurement requirement rather than a nicety.
Output quality trails Midjourney and Recraft. The trade is aesthetics for legal cover — the right trade on a client deliverable, the wrong one for a mood board.

entries.name: FLUX (Black Forest Labs)
entries.what: The image model family behind a large share of the tools on this list — released in open-weight and hosted variants, with per-image API pricing published from around $0.17.
entries.priceDetail: Open-weight variants free to run yourself. Hosted API priced per image, published from around $0.17 to $0.85 depending on the model.
notes: Worth knowing as the layer underneath: when three products claim different capabilities and all feel similar, it is often because they are all calling FLUX.
Open weights mean it can run on our own infrastructure through Replicate or Modal — the route when a client's imagery cannot go through a third-party product.
Licences differ by variant, and the permissive ones are not all commercial. Read the specific model's terms, not the family's.

entries.name: Playground
entries.what: Image generation aimed at graphics rather than art — logos, social posts and marketing assets with editable canvases and text handling, in a design-tool interface.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with daily limits. Paid at $12/month billed annually and $15/month monthly, with a $45/month tier.
notes: Text rendering and editable canvases put it closer to a design tool than a prompt box, which is why it survives a cut that removed twenty other image generators.
Rated Low: overlaps Recraft, which does vector output and holds a brand style better.
Generated graphics still need a designer's pass before a client sees them. Speed here mostly buys options to reject.

entries.name: Photoroom
entries.what: Product-photo editor — background removal and replacement, shadows, batch processing and templates, with an API for doing it at volume.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with watermark-free basics. Paid subscription plus API pricing per image.
notes: Better than Remove.bg on the whole job rather than just the cutout: shadows and consistent backgrounds are what make a client's product grid look deliberate.
The API and batch mode matter on e-commerce work, where the task is 400 images and not four.
Free tier is limited enough that any real project needs the subscription. Cheap against a photographer's retouching invoice.

entries.name: Clipdrop
entries.what: Suite of one-job image tools in one place — background removal, cleanup, uncrop, relight, upscale and sketch-to-image — with an API. Built by Stability AI.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with daily limits and watermarks on some tools. Paid subscription lifts both; API priced per call.
notes: Uncrop and relight are the two that solve real client problems — a supplied photo that is the wrong aspect ratio, or lit wrong for the layout.
Having them behind one login and one API beats collecting five single-purpose sites.
Quality is uneven tool to tool. Check the result at full size; the cleanup tool in particular leaves artefacts on complex backgrounds.

entries.name: Cleanup.pictures
entries.what: Removes objects, people and text from a photo by brushing over them, filling the gap from the surrounding image. One job, done in the browser.
entries.priceDetail: Free at reduced resolution. Paid from around $3/month for full resolution and higher-quality inpainting.
notes: The specific recurring job: a client photo with a competitor's logo, a stray sign or a bin in shot, needed today.
Free tier caps resolution, which is exactly where it stops being usable for a hero image — the paid tier is a few pounds.
Photoroom and Clipdrop both do this as part of a bigger suite. This is the one to send a client who needs to do it themselves once.

entries.name: Cody (Sourcegraph)
entries.what: Coding assistant built on Sourcegraph's code search, so its context is the whole indexed codebase rather than the open files — useful on repos too large for an editor to hold.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid from $16/user/month.
notes: Pick this one when the repo is genuinely big — a decade-old client monolith where Cursor's context window is the limiting factor. Code search is what Sourcegraph has always been good at.
Indexing a client repo puts a copy on their infrastructure. Worth the contract check before it points at anything private.

entries.name: Tabnine
entries.what: Code completion and chat with privacy as the product: air-gapped and on-premise deployment, models trained only on permissively licensed code, and provenance attribution on suggestions.
entries.priceDetail: Per-seat subscription; figures are not published on the pricing page — quoted on request.
notes: The differentiator is the licence story: trained on permissive code only, with attribution, which is the answer to a client asking whether our AI-written code could carry someone else's GPL.
Air-gapped deployment puts it alongside Tabby for regulated work. Tabby is open source and cheaper; Tabnine is the supported commercial version.

entries.name: Refact.ai
entries.what: Open-source coding agent for the IDE that runs the full loop — writes, runs tests, reads the failure, fixes — and can self-host the model alongside it.
entries.priceDetail: Open source and free to self-host. Hosted plan from $10/month.
notes: $10/month is the cheapest hosted agent on this list, which makes it the low-risk way to give someone here an agent without a $20 seat.
Self-hostable model plus agent in one package is unusual — the combination Tabby and Cline otherwise need two tools for.

entries.name: Blackbox AI
entries.what: Routes 300+ models through one endpoint, or runs an open-weight model of your choice as a dedicated deployment, with a coding assistant on top.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier at $0/month, then usage pricing with published per-million-token rates from around $0.26 to $4.40.
notes: The one-endpoint routing is the useful half: comparing models on the same prompt without holding five accounts and five keys.
Dedicated deployment of an open-weight model is the compliance option. Check what the shared routing tier does with prompts before using it on client code.

entries.name: Sourcery
entries.what: Automated code review in GitHub, GitLab or the IDE — comments on each pull request with concrete refactors rather than style nits.
entries.priceDetail: Free for open-source and small use. Paid at $12 and $24/user/month.
notes: The cheapest of the three reviewers here — $12 against CodeRabbit's $24 and Greptile's $30 — and enough for a small team that wants a second pair of eyes on every PR.
Narrower than the others: strong on refactoring suggestions, weaker on cross-repo reasoning and security.

entries.name: Jules
entries.what: Google's asynchronous coding agent — hand it a task against a GitHub repo and it works in a cloud VM, returning a plan and a pull request to review.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with daily task limits; higher limits come with paid Google AI subscriptions. No standalone price published.
notes: Free daily tasks make it the cheapest async agent to try — good for the backlog chores nobody wants: dependency bumps, test coverage, small refactors.
Cloud VMs mean client code on Google's infrastructure, and the free tier's terms are worth reading before that happens.

entries.name: Tempo
entries.what: Turns customer feedback, issues and requirements into reviewed pull requests — agents do the implementation and the team approves, so the queue is the input rather than a prompt.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier; paid plan figures are not published on the pricing page.
notes: The interesting bit is the input: pointing agents at a real backlog rather than at a chat box is closer to how client work actually arrives.
Rated Low because it wants to own the whole intake-to-PR flow, and ours runs through Foundry. Pricing is also unpublished.

entries.name: Create
entries.what: Prompt-to-app builder that generates a working full-stack site or tool with database and auth wired up, editable in the browser and deployable from it.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid at $19/month and $199/month, with $60 and $480 annual figures on the pricing page.
notes: An option alongside Bolt and Replit for a pitch prototype. Its differentiator is generating the backend pieces rather than only the front end.
Rated Low against v0 and Bolt: the output is further from a codebase we would keep, and the $199 tier is steep for a sketchpad.

entries.name: Rork
entries.what: Builds cross-platform mobile apps from a prompt using React Native and Expo, with publishing to the App Store and Play Store from the same place.
entries.priceDetail: Subscription tiers; figures are not published in the served pricing page.
notes: React Native and Expo output is the reason this beats FlutterFlow for us — it lands in the stack we already use, and Expo is already on this list.
App-store publishing from a prompt tool sounds better than it is; review, signing and store policy are still ours. Pricing is unpublished.

entries.name: Mistral
entries.what: European model lab with open-weight and commercial models, an API, fine-tuning, and Le Chat as the consumer surface — plus on-premise deployment for regulated work.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier on Le Chat. Paid consumer plans at $14.99 and $24.99/user/month; API billed per token, with enterprise deployment quoted separately. Several models released under Apache 2.0.
notes: The EU-hosted option, which matters more than its benchmark scores: a UK or EU client asking where inference happens gets a straight answer, and GDPR conversations get shorter.
Apache-2.0 weights on several models mean the same family can run locally through Ollama and hosted in production — one prompt, two deployment stories.

entries.name: Cohere
entries.what: Model provider aimed squarely at enterprise retrieval — strong embedding and rerank models, private deployment into a customer's own cloud, and multilingual coverage.
entries.priceDetail: Free trial keys. Production billed per token, with published rates from around $0.30 to $2.00 per million; enterprise deployment quoted separately.
notes: Their rerank model is the practical reason to know them: dropping it in front of a retrieval pipeline usually improves answer quality more than swapping the generation model.
Deployment into a client's own VPC is the selling point for regulated work. Overkill for anything smaller.

entries.name: Together AI
entries.what: Hosts open models for inference, fine-tuning and dedicated GPU clusters behind an OpenAI-compatible API, covering hundreds of open-weight models.
entries.priceDetail: Per-token inference with published rates from around $0.06 to $3.48 per million, plus hourly GPU cluster pricing.
notes: The breadth is the point: when a project needs one specific open model, this is more likely to carry it than Groq's curated list.
Fine-tuning on the same platform as serving is convenient. Check licence terms of the base model before shipping a fine-tune in a client product.

entries.name: Fireworks AI
entries.what: Inference and fine-tuning platform for open models, tuned for low latency and high throughput, with function calling and structured output support.
entries.priceDetail: Free credits to start. Per-token pricing from around $0.008 to $0.50 per million depending on model size, plus dedicated deployments.
notes: Structured-output and function-calling support on open models is the useful part — that is usually what breaks when moving a feature off a frontier model to save cost.
Direct alternative to Together and Groq. Pick on the specific model and latency you need, not on the brand.

entries.name: Baseten
entries.what: Deploys custom and open-source models as production endpoints with autoscaling, and handles the packaging so a model becomes an API without writing serving code.
entries.priceDetail: Free credits. Usage-based from around $0.30 per compute-hour unit, with published figures at $3.00 and $15.00 tiers.
notes: The option when a client project needs a bespoke or fine-tuned model in production rather than an off-the-shelf one — the case Replicate handles less well.
More operational surface than Replicate. Only worth it when the model is genuinely ours to serve.

entries.name: RunPod
entries.what: On-demand and spot GPUs by the hour, plus serverless inference — the cheap end of renting compute, with per-second billing on serverless.
entries.priceDetail: Hourly GPU rates published from around $2.09 to $7.89 depending on card, with cheaper spot pricing and separate serverless rates.
notes: The cheapest way to get a real GPU for an afternoon — training a small model, batch-processing a client's image library, testing a local model at speed.
Raw infrastructure: you manage the container and the uptime. Modal or Replicate for anything that needs to stay up.

entries.name: Cerebras
entries.what: Runs open models on wafer-scale chips, producing token throughput far above GPU hosts, offered as an inference API and as training capacity.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with rate limits. Paid plans at $50/month and $200/month, with credit packs at $5, $10 and $48.
notes: Same argument as Groq — speed changes what an interaction can feel like — with a different curated model list, so it is worth knowing as the fallback.
Rated Low because Groq covers the same need and we have no volume that justifies two fast-inference accounts.

entries.name: Anyscale
entries.what: Managed Ray — the framework for distributing Python across a cluster — for data-heavy training, batch inference and pipelines that outgrow one machine.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Usage-based from around $3 per unit, with a $100 credit figure on the pricing page.
notes: Relevant only when a job is genuinely distributed — processing a client's entire media library, or training on more data than one GPU holds.
Rated Low: Modal covers our scale with far less ceremony. Know it exists for the job that outgrows Modal.

entries.name: Botpress
entries.what: Agent platform for customer support with a visual flow builder, knowledge bases, and deployment to web, WhatsApp, Slack and phone — priced by usage rather than per seat.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $25/month with usage add-ons, a $65 tier and $150/month for teams, plus around $0.65 per unit of AI spend.
notes: No per-seat cost is the practical difference on client work: a support agent handling a client's volume does not get more expensive as their team grows.
Multi-channel deployment — especially WhatsApp — is what clients actually ask for and what takes longest to build ourselves.

entries.name: Chatbase
entries.what: Builds a support agent from a website, docs or uploaded files and gives you an embeddable widget with analytics on what it could not answer.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $32/month and $120/month, with annual figures of $384 and $1,440.
notes: The most common small client ask on this whole list — "can we have a chatbot trained on our site" — answered in an afternoon rather than a sprint.
The unanswered-questions analytics is the part worth showing a client: it is a content gap report, not just a bot.

entries.name: Voiceflow
entries.what: Design-led platform for building chat and voice agents — a canvas for conversation flows with version control, testing and handoff to developers.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier to build. Paid team and enterprise plans; figures are not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Its strength is the design surface — a conversation flow a client can review before it is built, which is how we work on everything else.
Pricing unpublished, and it aims at enterprise. Prototype on the free tier before quoting anything.

entries.name: Retell AI
entries.what: Voice agent platform with per-minute billing — telephony, low-latency speech, and a test-and-monitor surface for production phone agents.
entries.priceDetail: Free credits to start, then around $0.07 per minute, with a $10 starting credit and published rates down to $0.002 per unit at volume.
notes: Directly comparable to Vapi and worth pricing against it on a real client job — per-minute rates differ enough to matter at volume.
Its testing tools are better than most: simulating calls before a client's phone line goes live is the difference between a demo and a deployment.

entries.name: Bland
entries.what: Voice agents with self-hosted models and sub-second latency, aimed at high call volume with enterprise compliance options.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. From $15/month, with per-minute rates published around $0.05 to $0.14.
notes: Third option alongside Vapi and Retell, and the one that claims its own model hosting rather than stitching third-party speech services together — fewer moving parts, less latency.
Same standing caveat on all three: cap spend and call length before a phone line goes live, and get caller disclosure into the client's scope.

entries.name: Langflow
entries.what: Open-source visual builder for LLM pipelines and agents, Python-native underneath, so a flow can be exported and run as code rather than trapped in the canvas.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source; a hosted option exists through DataStax.
notes: Exporting to Python is the reason to pick it over Flowise for anything that might graduate: the prototype becomes the starting code rather than being rebuilt.
Backed by DataStax, so it has a company behind it — unusual among the visual builders.

entries.name: MindStudio
entries.what: No-code builder for AI workflows and agents that publishes as a shareable app, browser extension or API, with model choice per step.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $16 and $20/month, with a $24/month team tier.
notes: Cheap enough to put an internal tool in a non-developer's hands here — a repeatable client-report generator, say — without it becoming a build.
Per-step model choice keeps cost sane: a cheap model for extraction, an expensive one only where judgement is needed.

entries.name: Manus
entries.what: General-purpose agent that executes multi-step tasks in its own cloud environment — browses, writes files, runs code — and returns finished work rather than instructions.
entries.priceDetail: Credit-based subscription; figures are not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Worth knowing because clients ask about it by name. Its useful shape for us is research and data-gathering tasks, not code we would ship.
Rated Low: unpublished pricing, and Claude Code already does the parts of this we need with our own supervision.

entries.name: Budibase
entries.what: Open-source internal-tool builder — connect a database or API, generate CRUD screens and forms, add automations, and self-host the whole thing.
entries.priceDetail: Open source and free to self-host. Paid from $5/user/month, with $19, $49 and $299/month tiers for hosted and enterprise features.
notes: The open-source answer to Retool, and the one to reach for when a client's data cannot leave their infrastructure or they baulk at per-seat SaaS.
Less polished than Retool and the component set is narrower. Fine for admin panels; not for a customer-facing product.

entries.name: Softr
entries.what: Builds client portals and internal tools on top of Airtable, Google Sheets or a database — permissions, branded pages and forms without code.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid from $19/month, with $99/month for business features and per-user add-ons around $5–$10.
notes: Directly useful for agency work: a branded client portal over data already in Airtable, live in a day, for less than a day of our time.
Airtable-shaped, so it inherits Airtable's record limits and per-seat costs. Check both before proposing it as permanent.

entries.name: Noloco
entries.what: Client-portal and internal-tool builder over Airtable, Postgres or Google Sheets, with granular per-record permissions and white-labelling.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid from $79/month, with per-user pricing around $6 above the included seats.
notes: Stronger permission model than Softr, which is what matters when several of a client's customers each see only their own records.
At $79/month it is the dearer of the two. Worth it when the permissions are the requirement rather than the look.

entries.name: WeWeb
entries.what: No-code front-end builder that produces a real web app against your own backend — Supabase, Xano or any REST API — and exports to self-hosting.
entries.priceDetail: Free to build. Paid plans per project; figures are not published in the served pricing page.
notes: The bring-your-own-backend model is why this beats Bubble for us: the data layer stays somewhere we can own, version and migrate.
Self-hosted export means a client is not trapped. Pricing is unpublished, so get it in writing before scoping.

entries.name: Base44
entries.what: Prompt-to-app platform with database, auth and hosting included — describe the tool, get a working app, iterate in chat. Now owned by Wix.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $16, $40, $80 and $160/month.
notes: The $16 entry tier makes it the cheapest of the prompt-to-app tools for a genuinely internal tool nobody will maintain.
Rated Low: Wix acquisition means the roadmap now serves Wix, and there is no code export worth the name.

entries.name: Durable
entries.what: Generates a small-business website in about a minute, then bundles the surrounding admin — invoicing, CRM and SEO tooling — around it.
entries.priceDetail: Free to build. Paid from around $2/month promotional up to $25/month, with a $20/month standard tier.
notes: Worth knowing as the honest answer to an enquiry we should not take: a sole trader wanting a five-page site does not need a studio.
Rated Low as a tool for us — the output is template-grade and there is nothing to hand over.

entries.name: Hex
entries.what: Collaborative data notebooks — SQL and Python in the same document, published as an interactive app so a stakeholder gets a dashboard rather than a notebook.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid from around $100/month, with usage components published from $0.32 per unit.
notes: The publish-as-app step is the differentiator: analysis for a client ends up as something they can use, not a notebook they cannot open.
Priced for data teams, which we are not. Reach for it on a project where analysis is the deliverable.

entries.name: Deepnote
entries.what: Collaborative Python and SQL notebooks in the browser with real-time editing, scheduling and shareable dashboards, and no local environment to set up.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid at $39 and $50/month per user, with a $112/month team tier and $280 annual figure.
notes: Cheaper than Hex and better for the collaborative middle: two people poking at a client's data without arguing about Python versions.
Notebooks still rot. Anything a client depends on should graduate into code in their repo.

entries.name: Rows
entries.what: Spreadsheet with live integrations built in — pull from 50+ sources including databases, analytics and APIs into cells, then publish the sheet as a dashboard.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $8/month per user (or $6 annual) and $79/month for teams.
notes: The fastest route to a client-facing metrics view that we do not have to maintain: the integrations are the product, and it publishes as a page.
A spreadsheet is still a spreadsheet. Fine for a monthly report, wrong as a client's operational system.

entries.name: Julius
entries.what: Chat interface over your own data files — upload a spreadsheet or connect a database and it writes and runs the analysis, returning charts and the code it used.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $16 and $20/month, with a $45/month tier.
notes: Showing the code it ran is what makes it trustworthy — the analysis is checkable rather than a chart you have to believe.
$20/month against a day of someone here fighting a client's CSV export is an easy trade.

entries.name: Equals
entries.what: Spreadsheet with a live SQL connection to your database, built so a model can refresh from source rather than living on a stale export.
entries.priceDetail: Paid from $24/month per user (or $36 monthly), with team tiers at $250 and $500/month.
notes: Solves the real spreadsheet failure — the numbers were right the day it was made — by keeping the connection to the database live.
Rated Low: aimed at finance teams, and we do not build financial models. Rows covers our lighter version of this.

entries.name: Adobe Express
entries.what: Adobe's browser design tool — templates, brand kits, background removal and Firefly generation, with the Creative Cloud asset library behind it.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with a large template and asset set. Paid tier included with Creative Cloud; standalone figures not published in the served page.
notes: The option to hand a client already inside Adobe: brand kits carry over from their existing assets, which Canva cannot do.
Firefly generation inside it inherits Adobe's licensed training data, so client-facing output has the same legal cover as Firefly itself.

entries.name: Microsoft Designer
entries.what: Free browser design tool for social posts and graphics with generative fill and image creation, wired into Microsoft 365 and OneDrive.
entries.priceDetail: Free with a Microsoft account; higher limits with Microsoft 365.
notes: The free option for a client on Microsoft 365 who will not pay for Canva — their licence probably already covers it.
Rated Low: template quality trails Canva and Express, and output needs restyling before it represents a brand we built.

entries.name: Kittl
entries.what: Vector design tool in the browser aimed at type-led and print work — lettering effects, textures, mockups and a large licensed asset library, with real vector export.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid subscription with figures on the pricing page including a $200 tier and $4,185/year enterprise figure; per-seat monthly figures were not in the served HTML.
notes: Genuinely good at the thing Canva is bad at: display lettering and print-ready vector work, with merch mockups built in.
Vector export means output can go into a real brand system rather than staying a PNG. Confirm the per-seat price in-app before buying.

entries.name: Lovart
entries.what: Design agent that takes a brand description and produces a whole set — logo, packaging, social content and video ads — in one conversation, on an editable canvas.
entries.priceDetail: Free credits to start; paid tiers not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Worth knowing because it is the clearest example of what clients now expect a design agent to do, and a useful thing to be able to talk about accurately.
Rated Low: output is generic and unusable as identity work. The value is speed on throwaway variations, not a brand.

entries.name: Polymet
entries.what: Generates production-ready product designs and matching front-end code from a description or a reference image, working against a design system rather than from scratch.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier; paid figures not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Another option in the same lane as Subframe and Magic Patterns. Its angle is full product screens rather than single components.
Pricing unpublished, which is common in this category and a reason to trial rather than commit.

entries.name: Visily
entries.what: Wireframing tool that converts a screenshot, sketch or text prompt into an editable hi-fidelity design, with prototyping and a large template set.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $11/month and $29/month.
notes: Cheaper than Uizard at $11 and better at the screenshot-to-editable trick, which is the one genuinely useful feature in this category.
Rated Low for the same reason as Uizard: we have designers. Its use is capturing a client's own sketch before kickoff.

entries.name: Flair
entries.what: Drag-and-drop AI editor for product photography — place a product on a generated set with controlled lighting and composition, then batch out variations.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $8, $26 and $38/month.
notes: Real client use on e-commerce work: a product shot in five settings without booking a studio, from one clean cut-out.
At $8/month it is worth trying against Photoroom. Flair is stronger on composed scenes, Photoroom on volume.

entries.name: Mockey
entries.what: Free mockup generator with 30,000+ templates — apparel, print, packaging and devices — upload a design and download the composite.
entries.priceDetail: Free with no watermark on the base library; paid tier for premium templates and bulk export.
notes: Fills the merch and print gap Rotato does not touch: t-shirts, tote bags, packaging and signage for a brand project.
Templates are template-grade. Fine for a client presentation, not for a hero image on a launch site.

entries.name: Synthesia
entries.what: Generates presenter-led video from a script using avatars and voices in 140+ languages, with brand templates and a screen-recording mode.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier with limited minutes. Paid at $18/month, $29/month and $89/month per seat.
notes: The one AI video tool with a real client use case for us: training and onboarding video that has to exist in eight languages and be updated when the process changes.
Avatars still read as avatars. Right for internal and instructional content, wrong for anything brand-led.

entries.name: HeyGen
entries.what: Avatar video generation with translation and lip-sync — record once and produce the same video in dozens of languages, or build an avatar from a real presenter.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $29, $49 and $149/month.
notes: The translation-with-lip-sync is the differentiator against Synthesia: an existing client video localised rather than regenerated from a script.
Cloning a real person's likeness needs written consent from that person, not just from the client. Get it in the scope.

entries.name: Kapwing
entries.what: Browser video editor with the utility layer teams actually need — auto-subtitles, resizing for each platform, background removal and a full project from one prompt.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier with watermarks on some exports. Paid at $16, $24 and $50/month.
notes: Nothing to install, which makes it the one to send a client who needs to trim and caption a video themselves.
Overlaps VEED closely. Kapwing is a little stronger on templates, VEED on dubbing — try both on the same clip.

entries.name: VEED
entries.what: Browser video editor with AI dubbing, subtitles, eye-contact correction and filler-word removal, plus a screen recorder.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with watermarks. Paid subscription tiers; per-seat figures were not in the served pricing page.
notes: Dubbing is the reason to keep it alongside Kapwing — a client video into another language without re-shooting or paying a voice artist.
Free tier watermarks output, so any real use is paid. Confirm the current figure in-app.

entries.name: Opus Clip
entries.what: Cuts long video into short vertical clips, choosing moments by predicted engagement, then adds captions, reframes to keep the speaker centred and schedules the posts.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with monthly minute limits. Paid at $15/month and $29/month.
notes: The best of a crowded category and the only one worth listing: auto-reframing that tracks the speaker is what makes the output usable without a manual pass.
Its use for us is turning a client webinar or podcast into a month of social content — a deliverable we can sell, not just a tool.

entries.name: Submagic
entries.what: Adds the short-form video treatment automatically — animated captions, b-roll, zooms, sound effects and hooks — from an uploaded clip.
entries.priceDetail: Free trial. Paid at $19, $38, $39 and $58/month depending on volume.
notes: Does one job well: the caption-and-b-roll style short-form video now expects, in a minute rather than an hour of editing.
Rated Low because the style is aggressively of-the-moment and will date. Use it for a client's social feed, never for brand film.

entries.name: Pika
entries.what: Generative video from text, image or video input, with editing controls for extending clips, swapping elements and applying effects to a region.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier with limited credits. Paid at $8, $28 and $76/month.
notes: Cheapest way into generative video at $8/month — useful for a moodboard or a motion test before committing to Runway.
Rated Low against Runway: less control and no real editing surface. An option for exploration, not delivery.

entries.name: Luma Dream Machine
entries.what: Generative video and image platform from Luma, with camera-motion control, keyframe-to-keyframe generation and a reference-image workflow.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with limited generations. Paid at $30/month and $90/month, with annual figures of $300 and $900.
notes: Camera-motion control is its differentiator — specifying a dolly or an orbit rather than hoping the model chooses one.
Rated Low: $30/month for exploratory footage is hard to justify against Runway's editing surface at a similar price.

entries.name: Stability AI
entries.what: The company behind Stable Diffusion — open-weight image, video, audio and 3D models, plus a hosted API and enterprise licences for self-hosting.
entries.priceDetail: Free non-commercial use of many models. Paid API credits, with a $19/month creator tier and $50/month professional tier; enterprise licences quoted separately.
notes: The reason to know them is licensing, not quality: their open weights are what make on-premise image generation possible for a client who cannot use a hosted model.
Read the specific model licence. Several are free for non-commercial use only, and revenue thresholds apply to the commercial tiers.

entries.name: Civitai
entries.what: Community hub for open image models — thousands of Stable Diffusion and FLUX checkpoints and LoRAs, with example outputs and the settings that produced them.
entries.priceDetail: Free browsing and downloads. Paid tiers at $10, $25 and $50/month for on-site generation.
notes: Where you find a LoRA trained on a specific style or product type — genuinely useful when a client needs consistent imagery in one visual language.
Rated Low deliberately: much of the site is adult content and model provenance is unverifiable. Download to our own pipeline, do not browse it on a client's screen.

entries.name: OpenArt
entries.what: One interface over 100+ image and video models from Google, OpenAI, Seedream and others, with character consistency tools and a shared prompt library.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with daily credits. Paid at $14/month and $34/month, with per-seat annual figures of $13 and $27.
notes: Model breadth under one subscription is the practical case: comparing four models on the same brief without four accounts.
Character-consistency tooling is the feature worth testing — keeping the same person or product across a set is where most generated imagery falls apart.

entries.name: Lexica
entries.what: Searchable archive of millions of generated images with the prompts that made them, plus its own generation model.
entries.priceDetail: Free search. Paid generation tiers; figures not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Use it as reverse prompt engineering: find an image close to the look you want and read the prompt that produced it, instead of guessing.
Faster than iterating from scratch, and free for the search half — which is the half worth having.

entries.name: PromptHero
entries.what: Searchable prompt library across Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and DALL·E outputs, with courses and a model-specific prompt-building guide.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month tier. Paid at $16/month and $24/month, with a $194/year option.
notes: The teaching angle is the value — prompt structure per model, which is the bit people here learn by trial and error.
Rated Low: Lexica covers the search half for free. This is worth it only if someone wants the structured learning.

entries.name: Reve
entries.what: Image model with natural-language editing — describe a change and it edits the existing image rather than regenerating it, with strong prompt adherence and text rendering.
entries.priceDetail: Free credits to start; paid tiers not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Edit-by-instruction is the workflow that matters for client work: changing one element of an approved image without losing everything else about it.
Genuinely good at text inside images, which most models still fail at. Pricing unpublished — try the free credits first.

entries.name: Topaz Labs
entries.what: Professional photo and video enhancement — upscaling, denoise, sharpen and frame interpolation, running locally as desktop apps with plugin versions for Adobe tools.
entries.priceDetail: Perpetual licences with published figures at $19 and $39, plus a $12/month subscription option.
notes: The professional standard for rescuing supplied assets — the 800px logo that must be a billboard, or client footage shot at the wrong frame rate.
Runs locally, so unreleased client material never leaves the machine. Perpetual licence rather than a subscription, which is rare and worth it.

entries.name: Pixelcut
entries.what: Product-photo toolkit — background removal and replacement, object erase, upscale and batch processing — with a mobile app and an API.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $8/month annual, $10/month monthly, and a $30/month tier.
notes: Cheapest credible option in this cluster at $8/month, with an API — the one to reach for when the job is volume rather than craft.
Mobile app matters more than it sounds: a client can shoot and clean up their own product photos on a phone.

entries.name: Let's Enhance
entries.what: Upscaling and enhancement in the browser with an API — resolution, lighting and colour correction, plus batch processing and a print-size mode.
entries.priceDetail: Free credits to start. Paid at $9, $12, $24 and $32/month depending on volume.
notes: Browser-based with an API, so it covers the case Topaz does not: upscaling inside an automated pipeline rather than on someone's desktop.
Rated Low: Topaz is better on quality and Upscayl is free locally. This wins only when it has to run server-side.

entries.name: Adobe Podcast
entries.what: Audio cleanup that makes a phone or laptop recording sound like it was recorded in a studio — removes room noise and reverb, evens levels, and transcribes.
entries.priceDetail: Free with an Adobe account; Enhance Speech has generous free limits.
notes: Directly fixes the weak link in everything we record: a walkthrough or client interview recorded on a laptop mic in a normal room. One pass and it is presentable.
Free, browser-based and better at de-reverberation than the paid tools bundled into editors. Run recordings through it before they reach Descript.

entries.name: AIVA
entries.what: Generates original music by style and duration, with a licence to use the output — including options that assign full copyright of the generated track.
entries.priceDetail: Free €0 tier for non-commercial use. Paid at €11/month and €33/month, the higher tier including copyright ownership of generated tracks.
notes: Solves a real recurring cost: background music for a client video without a stock-library subscription or a sync-licence conversation.
The licensing tiers are the whole point — the free tier is non-commercial, and only the top tier assigns ownership. Read which one a client deliverable needs.

entries.name: Otter.ai
entries.what: Real-time meeting transcription with live chat, summaries and action items, joining Zoom, Meet and Teams as a bot.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with monthly minute limits. Paid at $8/user/month annual ($16 monthly), $30/month for business, and around $24/user for enterprise.
notes: The incumbent, and the one a client is most likely to already have — worth knowing so we do not propose a second transcriber into their stack.
$8/user annual is the cheapest paid option in this cluster. Weakest of them on summary quality.

entries.name: Fireflies
entries.what: Meeting recorder that pushes what it captures outward — CRM updates, task creation and workflow automations across email, chat and connected apps.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $10/user/month annual ($18 monthly), $19 and $29/month for higher tiers.
notes: The automation layer is why to pick this one: a client call that ends with the CRM already updated and tasks created, rather than notes to process later.
Integration depth is also the risk — it reaches into a lot of systems. Scope its permissions before connecting it to anything client-facing.

entries.name: Circleback
entries.what: Meeting notes built for accuracy and structure rather than volume — clean summaries, extracted action items with owners, and automations, across any platform.
entries.priceDetail: $20.83/user/month billed annually, or $25/user/month monthly. No free tier.
notes: Notably better output quality than the cheap end of this cluster — the summaries need less editing before they go to a client.
No free tier and the dearest per seat here. Justified only if the notes actually get sent to clients as-is.

entries.name: Bluedot
entries.what: Bot-free meeting recorder — a Chrome extension captures the call without joining it, so nothing announces itself to the other participants. Handles in-person meetings too.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/user tier. Paid at $14, $18, $20 and $32/user/month.
notes: Bot-free is the same argument as Granola, with in-person meeting capture on top — useful for a client workshop where no call is happening.
No visible bot does not remove the duty to tell people they are being recorded. Say it at the top of the call.

entries.name: Jamie
entries.what: Bot-free note-taker built in Germany with EU data residency — records from the device across any platform, including offline meetings, and outputs structured notes.
entries.priceDetail: Free €0 tier. Paid at €21/month annual, €33/month and €39/month.
notes: EU data residency is the reason it is here: for a UK or EU client asking where recordings of their meetings are stored, this is the straightforward answer.
Priced in euros and slightly dearer than the US options. The compliance answer is what you are paying for.

entries.name: tl;dv
entries.what: Records and transcribes Zoom, Meet and Teams with timestamped highlights and clips, so a specific thirty seconds of a client call can be shared rather than the whole recording.
entries.priceDetail: Genuinely usable free tier with unlimited recordings and transcripts. Paid tiers for CRM integrations and analytics.
notes: Best free tier in this cluster — unlimited recording and transcription at $0, which is enough for a studio our size.
Clipping a moment out of a call is the underrated feature: sending a client's own words to the team beats paraphrasing them.

entries.name: Tactiq
entries.what: Browser-extension transcription that runs on the call you are already in — no bot joins, transcripts appear live, and summaries generate from a prompt you control.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier with monthly transcript limits. Paid at $8, $16.67 and $29.17/month.
notes: Lightest option here — an extension rather than a service that stores everything, which makes it the easiest to get past a client's IT.
Custom summary prompts mean output can match how we actually write notes rather than a generic template.

entries.name: Semantic Scholar
entries.what: Free academic search across 200 million-plus papers from the Allen Institute, with citation context, influential-citation ranking and a public API.
entries.priceDetail: Free, including the API.
notes: Free API is the part worth remembering: if a client project ever needs literature search built in, this is the source that does not bill per query.
Non-profit and stable, unlike most of this category. No sales motion, no pivot risk.

entries.name: Connected Papers
entries.what: Builds a visual graph of papers related to one you already have, by citation similarity rather than keyword — so the field around a paper becomes visible at a glance.
entries.priceDetail: Free for basic use, with a paid tier for heavy users.
notes: The graph view answers a question search cannot: what else sits around this idea, including work that uses different vocabulary.
Rated Low — we rarely do literature work. Genuinely good when a client claim needs an evidence base.

entries.name: ResearchRabbit
entries.what: Literature discovery that learns from a starting set of papers and keeps recommending, with collaborative collections and citation network views.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid from around $10/month, with a $12.50 tier.
notes: Recommendation-based rather than one-shot search, which suits an ongoing subject rather than a single question.
Rated Low for the same reason as Connected Papers: real capability, rare need.

entries.name: Humata
entries.what: Turns uploaded documents into a queryable knowledge base with page-level citations, aimed at long technical and legal documents.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $9/month and $49/user/month, with usage priced around $0.02 per page.
notes: The paid option next to NotebookLM, with page-level citations and per-page pricing that suits one big document rather than a whole corpus.
Uploading a client's contracts or specs is a processing decision. NotebookLM's Workspace terms are usually easier to defend.

entries.name: PDF.ai
entries.what: Chat with a PDF — ask questions, get summaries and cited answers — with an API for doing it inside another product.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with document limits; paid subscription figures not published in the served page.
notes: The API is the only interesting part for us: document Q&A as a feature in a client build, without assembling a retrieval stack.
Rated Low, and honestly a weekend build with Firecrawl and an embedding model if a client needs it properly.

entries.name: You.com
entries.what: Search API and assistant aimed at giving agents web results with citations, including a research endpoint that returns structured reports.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. API billed per query, with published figures from around $1.00 to $12.00 per thousand and a $100 credit tier.
notes: Second option next to Exa for giving an agent live web access — worth pricing both against a real workload, as their per-query rates differ.
Cap usage before wiring it into anything automated. A looping agent on a per-query API is a bill, not an error.

entries.name: Superhuman
entries.what: Keyboard-first email client built for speed — split inboxes, snippets, send-later and AI drafting, over Gmail or Outlook.
entries.priceDetail: Per-seat subscription; figures are not published in the served pricing page.
notes: Worth it for whoever here carries the client correspondence — the whole product is removing seconds from an action performed a hundred times a day.
Unpublished pricing and historically expensive. It only pays back for someone genuinely living in email.

entries.name: Notion Calendar
entries.what: Calendar client tied into Notion — joins meetings in a click, shows availability for scheduling links, and surfaces Notion pages against events.
entries.priceDetail: Free with a Notion account. Paid Notion plans at $10 and $20/user/month, with a $8/month annual figure.
notes: Free and better than the native calendar apps at the two things that matter daily: joining the right call and sharing availability without a scheduling tool.
Formerly Cron, which is the row this replaced in the audit. Anything pointing at cron.com is stale.

entries.name: Sunsama
entries.what: Daily planner that pulls tasks from Jira, Linear, Asana, Trello and email into one deliberate daily plan, with a guided shutdown at the end of the day.
entries.priceDetail: $17/month billed annually or $22/month monthly, with a $24.99 figure on the pricing page. Free trial, no free tier.
notes: Aggregating across trackers is the point for us: work arrives from a client's Jira, our own tickets and email, and this makes one list out of three.
No free tier and $17/month is dear for a planner. It suits people who plan a day deliberately and is wasted on anyone who does not.

entries.name: Reclaim
entries.what: Calendar automation — defends focus time, schedules habits and tasks into real gaps, and reshuffles automatically when a meeting lands on top of them.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid at $8, $16, $24 and $32/user/month.
notes: Automatic rescheduling is what separates it from a planner: on a week where client calls keep landing, the focus blocks move themselves instead of being deleted.
Now owned by Dropbox. Free tier is enough to find out whether the automation suits how someone works.

entries.name: Todoist
entries.what: Task manager with natural-language input, projects, labels and filters, on every platform, with a genuinely capable free tier.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with project limits. Paid tiers per user; figures not published in the served page.
notes: The default personal task list, and the one whose quick-add is fast enough to actually capture things — "call the client tomorrow at 10" parses correctly.
Personal, not project management. Client work belongs in Foundry; this is for the things that fall between.

entries.name: Trello
entries.what: Kanban boards with automation, checklists and integrations — the simplest shared board a client will actually keep using.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier with unlimited cards. Paid at $5, $6 and $10/user/month.
notes: Its use is client-facing simplicity: a shared board for approvals or content collection that a non-technical client can operate without training.
Rated Low internally — we run on Foundry — but worth having as the answer when a client insists on their own board.

entries.name: Tana
entries.what: Structured notes with typed nodes and fields, now positioned around meetings — agents create structured records during the call rather than after it.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $20, $30 and $80/month.
notes: Typed nodes mean notes become data — every client meeting a record with the same fields, queryable later. Powerful and genuinely different from a document.
Rated Low: a steep learning curve, and the structure only pays back if someone maintains it. Hejour is the simpler daily-notes option already listed.

entries.name: Reflect
